examples.problem_statement: Which of the parentheses in the following expressions could be removed without changing the value of the expression and are therefore unnecessary? (a) -(5^2) - (12 - 7)   (b) (x + y) - (w + z) - (a \times b)

solution.operation: -(5^2): exponent before negation and before subtraction
solution.description: Check the parentheses around the squared term: exponentiation already outranks both the negation and the subtraction, so grouping it changes nothing and the parentheses can be dropped.
Evaluate the second expression as it is printed: the parentheses force 7 to be subtracted from 12 first, giving 5, which is then subtracted from 25 to yield 20.
Now delete those parentheses and work strictly left to right; the value drops to 6, so the value did change and the parentheses around 12 - 7 are necessary.

solution.operation: (x + y) - \ldots : addition and subtraction run left to right
solution.result: the parentheses around x + y are unnecessary
solution.description: Look at the leading group in (b): addition and subtraction are performed left to right by default, so x + y is already computed before the neighboring subtraction and the parentheses add nothing.

solution.result: the parentheses around a \times b are unnecessary
solution.description: Look at the trailing group: multiplication is the first operation performed anyway, so surrounding a \times b with parentheses does not change the order and they can be removed.

solution.result: the parentheses around w + z are necessary
solution.description: Test the middle group: with the parentheses you subtract both w and z, but without them you would subtract w and add z, so this pair must stay.

key_reminders: Exponents are evaluated before negation and before addition or subtraction.
Multiplication outranks addition and subtraction, so parentheses around a product next to a sum are redundant.
A minus sign in front of a parenthesized sum distributes to every term inside it.
common_mistakes: Dropping the parentheses in 25 - (12 - 7) and computing left to right to get 6 instead of 20.
Removing the parentheses in -(w + z) and then adding z instead of subtracting it.

concept.technique_name: symmetric cancellation of a consecutive-integer sum about zero

examples.problem_statement: What is the sum of all the integers from -457 to 459, inclusive?

solution.operation: recognize that adding 917 terms one by one is not feasible; test a smaller analogue, the sum from -2 to 4
solution.description: Since summing this many numbers directly is impossible under test conditions, look for the trick by shrinking the range to a case small enough to add by hand.
In the small case, pair each negative with its positive twin: each pair sums to zero, and the 0 in the middle contributes nothing, so the symmetric block vanishes.
Add only the leftover terms past the symmetric block; their total is the whole sum, confirming that the sum equals the unpaired tail.
Carry the pattern to the real range: every integer from -457 up to 457 pairs off with its opposite and cancels, leaving only the terms above 457.
Add the two surviving integers at the top of the range to get the sum of the entire list.

key_reminders: Any integer and its opposite sum to zero, so a range symmetric about 0 contributes nothing.
After cancelling the symmetric block, only the unpaired tail of the range remains to be added.
Testing the idea on a tiny analogous range confirms the pattern before applying it to large numbers.
common_mistakes: Cancelling only up to 456 or up to 458 and adding the wrong leftover terms (457 + 458 + 459 or just 459).
Treating the range as symmetric and answering 0 because the endpoints -457 and 459 look nearly balanced.

concept.technique_name: resolve-the-conflict argument evaluation with answer-choice elimination

examples.problem_statement:
The passage outlines a conflict between two standard theories - one of planet formation, the other of companion stars - and observations of one large body, and later two others, orbiting close to the star Upsilon Andromedae. Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the status of the orbiting body without casting doubt on the two standard theories mentioned?
(A) The smaller a planet orbiting a star is, and the farther away it is from the star, the less likely it is to be discovered.
(B) If a planet's orbit is disturbed, the planet can be drawn by gravity toward the star it is orbiting.
(C) The largest of the bodies orbiting Upsilon Andromedae is the farthest away from the star, and the smallest is the nearest.
(D) It is likely that there are many stars, in addition to Upsilon Andromedae and the Sun, that are orbited by more than one smaller body.
(E) In most cases of companion stars, the smaller companion is much fainter than the larger star.

solution.operation: state the conflict: two standard theories (planet formation, companion stars) versus the observation of large bodies orbiting close to the star
solution.result: a conflict between theory and observation
solution.description: Pin down what is actually at odds before reading the choices: the observed large bodies sit close to Upsilon Andromedae, which neither standard theory allows.

solution.operation: restate the task: find the choice that explains the observation while leaving both theories intact
solution.result: a two-part test each choice must pass
solution.description: Fix the criterion for a correct answer, because a choice that explains the observation by contradicting one of the theories fails the question's second requirement.

solution.operation: test (B): a planet may form far from a star and later be drawn closer
solution.result: (B) passes both parts of the test
solution.description: Apply the criterion to (B): if orbits can be disturbed inward, the close-in large bodies can be planets formed far out, so the observation is explained and the planet-formation theory survives; the companion-star theory is untouched as well.

solution.operation: test (A): difficulty of discovering a small, distant planet
solution.description: Reject (A) because it speaks to why small far-off planets go undetected, not to the status of a large body found near a star.

solution.operation: test (C): relative sizes and distances of the three bodies
solution.description: Reject (C) because whatever their relative size and position, all three bodies are still too close to the star for the standard theories, so the conflict remains.

solution.operation: test (D): many stars have more than one orbiting body
solution.description: Reject (D) because how common multi-body systems are says nothing about the status of the large bodies in question.

solution.operation: test (E): companion stars are usually much fainter
solution.description: Reject (E) as irrelevant: relative brightness of companion stars does not clarify what the large close-in bodies are.

examples.answer: Choice B: If a planet’s orbit is disturbed, the planet can be drawn by gravity toward the star it is orbiting.

key_reminders: The correct choice must both explain the observation and leave both stated theories standing.
A choice about detection difficulty or general prevalence does not bear on the status of a specific observed body.
Explaining an anomaly by a later change in circumstances (an orbit shifting inward) reconciles data with a formation theory instead of contradicting it.
common_mistakes: Picking (C) by treating the ordering of the three bodies as a resolution, when all three remain too close under both theories.
Picking (A) or (E) because they mention planets and companion stars, matching the passage's vocabulary rather than its conflict.
